title: "Hamiltonian Monte Carlo"

The random-walk version of [Metropolis--Hastings](metropolis-hastings.qmd)
proposes a nearby point without first asking how the posterior changes in that
direction. Making the proposal very small raises its chance of acceptance, but
the chain then crosses the posterior through many short, overlapping moves.
Making the proposal large reaches farther, but it also sends many proposals
into regions having very little posterior density. This is the **random-walk
problem**.

Can we use what we know about the posterior surface to choose a direction?
Yes. The [derivative discussion](../random-variables-and-distributions/expected-values.qmd#derivatives-as-local-rates-of-change)
defined a derivative as a local rate of change. For a function of several
parameters, the **gradient** collects one partial derivative for each
parameter. At a point $(\mu,\log\sigma)$, it tells us how the log posterior
would change under a small move in each coordinate. The
[posterior-geometry page](beyond-conjugacy.qmd#hessian-as-local-curvature)
introduced this vector and distinguished it from the Hessian, which records
how the local slopes themselves change.

[**Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC)**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-introstan.html)
uses the gradient to build a coordinated path through parameter space. It
augments the parameters with a temporary momentum, follows an approximate
trajectory, and then applies a Metropolis acceptance step to correct the small
error introduced by numerical calculation. The posterior remains the target
defined on the [posterior-distribution page](posterior-distributions.qmd).

What's going on mechanically? We will first translate the familiar idea of
moving along a slope into the position-and-momentum notation used by HMC. We
will then work through one leapfrog step before following a complete trajectory
through the passage-level Student-$t$ posterior.

## Potential, kinetic, and total energy

Imagine a ball in a smooth valley. Its **position** says where it is. Its
**momentum** combines a direction with an amount of motion. The height of the
valley determines **[potential energy](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-introstan.html)**,
while momentum determines **kinetic
energy**. As the ball moves uphill, kinetic energy is converted into potential
energy; as it moves downhill, potential energy is converted back into kinetic
energy.

HMC uses this picture as a computational construction. Low potential energy
will correspond to high posterior density, so the valley's low regions are
the parameter values the posterior supports most strongly. Momentum is an
auxiliary random variable used to move through the valley. It is freshly
generated during the transition and has no linguistic interpretation.

Let $q=(\mu,\lambda)$ denote the two unconstrained coordinates, where
$\lambda=\log\sigma$, and let $\rho$ be an auxiliary momentum. We use $q$
here because the mechanics notation treats the parameters as a position; the
coordinates themselves remain the familiar $\mu$ and $\log\sigma$. The
potential energy is

$$
U(q)=-\log\widetilde f(q\mid\mathbf y).
$$

For unit mass, draw $\rho\sim\mathcal N(0,I)$ and define

$$
K(\rho)=\frac12\rho^\mathsf T\rho,
\qquad
H(q,\rho)=U(q)+K(\rho).
$$

Adding the momentum does not change the marginal posterior for $q$. It supplies a direction in which to construct a proposal.

Hamilton's equations are

$$
\frac{\mathrm dq}{\mathrm dt}=\rho,
\qquad
\frac{\mathrm d\rho}{\mathrm dt}=-\nabla U(q).
$$

The first changes position using momentum; the second changes momentum using
the local posterior gradient. To read the second equation, recall that
$U(q)=-\log\widetilde f(q\mid\mathbf y)$. If moving to the right increases
$U$, then $\mathrm dU/\mathrm dq$ is positive and
$-\mathrm dU/\mathrm dq$ pushes the momentum left. The change in momentum
therefore points downhill in potential energy, which means uphill in log
posterior density.

In one dimension, imagine a ball moving across a valley whose height is
$U(q)$. The slope changes momentum, while momentum changes position. In more
than one dimension, $\nabla U(q)$ is the vector of slopes, one for each
coordinate.

### Where the passage-model gradient comes from

Stan will calculate the gradient automatically, but we should still know what
it is differentiating. Ignoring terms that do not depend on $\mu$ or $\sigma$,
the log density contributed by passage $j$ is

$$
\ell_j(\mu,\sigma)
=
-\log\sigma
-\frac{\nu+1}{2}
\log\left(
1+\frac{(y_j-\mu)^2}{\nu\sigma^2}
\right).
$$

This is simply the logarithm of the Student-$t$ density introduced on the
[model page](beyond-conjugacy.qmd#a-robust-location-scale-model), with the
constant terms removed. Taking logs converts the product of 55 likelihood
terms into a sum of 55 contributions.

Consider the derivative with respect to $\mu$. The term $-\log\sigma$ does not
change when $\mu$ changes, so its derivative is zero. The second term contains
$\mu$ through the squared residual $(y_j-\mu)^2$. Applying the chain rule gives

$$
\frac{\partial\ell_j}{\partial\mu}
=
\frac{(\nu+1)(y_j-\mu)}
{\nu\sigma^2+(y_j-\mu)^2}.
$$

The sign has a useful interpretation. If $y_j>\mu$, this passage contributes a
positive slope and pulls the location upward. If $y_j<\mu$, it contributes a
negative slope and pulls downward. The size of that pull decreases for an
extreme residual because the squared residual also appears in the denominator.
This is one way the Student-$t$ likelihood limits the influence of an extreme
passage.

Adding the 55 passage contributions and the derivative of the normal log
prior, $-\mu/s_\mu^2$, gives the $\mu$ component of the log-target gradient:

$$
\frac{\partial\log\widetilde f}{\partial\mu}
=
\sum_{j=1}^{55}
\frac{(\nu+1)(y_j-\mu)}{\nu\sigma^2+(y_j-\mu)^2}
-\frac{\mu}{s_\mu^2}.
$$

The summation is the Student-t likelihood contribution and the final term is
the normal-prior contribution. In the code, this is the first element returned
by `gradient_log_target()`.

The second coordinate used by HMC is $\lambda=\log\sigma$. Let
$r_j^2=(y_j-\mu)^2/\sigma^2$ denote the squared residual after scaling by
$\sigma$. Differentiating the full log target with respect to $\lambda$ gives

$$
\frac{\partial\log\widetilde f}{\partial\lambda}
=
\sum_{j=1}^{55}
\left[
-1+
\frac{(\nu+1)r_j^2}{\nu+r_j^2}
\right]
-\frac{\sigma^2}{s_\sigma^2}
+1.
$$

Within each likelihood contribution, $-1$ comes from $-\log\sigma$ and the
fraction comes from the residual term. The next term is the half-normal prior
contribution. The final $+1$ is the log-coordinate Jacobian derived in the
[local-stretching discussion](beyond-conjugacy.qmd#jacobians-as-local-stretching).
Thus both coordinates in the code correspond to a displayed derivative rather
than an unexplained software operation.

## Leapfrog integration

The differential equations describe continuous motion, but a computer must
replace that continuous path with finitely many calculations. We choose a
small **step size** $\epsilon$ and repeatedly update momentum and position.
This replacement of continuous motion by discrete numerical steps is called
**numerical integration**. The use of *integration* here concerns solving the
equations of motion; it is distinct from the posterior integration discussed
on the [Monte Carlo page](monte-carlo-integration.qmd#from-a-weighted-sum-to-a-draw-average).

For step size $\epsilon$, one leapfrog step is

$$
\rho_{t+\frac12}
=
\rho_t-\frac{\epsilon}{2}\nabla U(q_t),
$$

$$
q_{t+1}=q_t+\epsilon\rho_{t+\frac12},
$$

$$
\rho_{t+1}
=
\rho_{t+\frac12}-\frac{\epsilon}{2}\nabla U(q_{t+1}).
$$

Why split the momentum update into two halves? A full position step changes
the slope at which the next momentum update is calculated. Taking half of the
momentum update before that move and half after it treats the two ends
symmetrically. This symmetry makes it possible to reverse the calculation by
negating momentum and applying the same steps backward. The resulting
**[leapfrog integrator](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-introstan.html)**
is reversible and preserves volume in the augmented
position--momentum space, two properties required by the HMC transition.

Numerical integration changes the Hamiltonian slightly, so HMC accepts the endpoint with

$$
\alpha
=
\min\left\{1,
\exp[H(q,\rho)-H(q^*,\rho^*)]
\right\}.
$$

Thus one numerical step follows three visible operations: take half a momentum step using the gradient at $q_t$, take one position step using that updated momentum, then take the remaining half momentum step using the gradient at $q_{t+1}$. The code implements the two boundary half steps outside the loop and the intervening full momentum steps inside it.

## One trajectory through the passage-level Student-t model

The reference trajectory first whitens the grid posterior, then applies 12 leapfrog steps of size 0.20. Every potential and gradient evaluation still uses the observed 55-passage passage-level Student-t model. Whitening is a coordinate rescaling explained fully on the [mass-matrix page](mass-matrix-geometry.qmd#general-kinetic-energy): it makes the two posterior directions closer to comparable scales before a unit-mass trajectory is taken.

```{r}
#| label: provo-hmc-trajectory
#| code-fold: true
library(ggplot2)

provo <- read.csv("data/provo/passage-summaries.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
y <- provo$noun_minus_verb_log_ffd
nu <- 4
prior_scale <- 2 * sd(y)
log_sum_exp <- function(x) { m <- max(x); m + log(sum(exp(x - m))) }
log_target <- function(parameter_pair) {
  mu <- parameter_pair[1]; sigma <- exp(parameter_pair[2])
  sum(dt((y - mu) / sigma, df = nu, log = TRUE) - log(sigma)) +
    dnorm(mu, 0, prior_scale, log = TRUE) +
    log(2) + dnorm(sigma, 0, prior_scale, log = TRUE) + parameter_pair[2]
}
gradient_log_target <- function(parameter_pair) {
  mu <- parameter_pair[1]; sigma <- exp(parameter_pair[2]); residual <- y - mu
  scaled_squared <- residual^2 / sigma^2
  c(
    sum((nu + 1) * residual / (nu * sigma^2 + residual^2)) -
      mu / prior_scale^2,
    sum(-1 + (nu + 1) * scaled_squared / (nu + scaled_squared)) -
      sigma^2 / prior_scale^2 + 1
  )
}
mode_fit <- optim(c(median(y), log(mad(y))),
                  function(parameter_pair) -log_target(parameter_pair),
                  gr = function(parameter_pair) -gradient_log_target(parameter_pair),
                  method = "BFGS", hessian = TRUE,
                  control = list(reltol = 1e-12, maxit = 1000L))
local_sd <- sqrt(diag(solve(mode_fit$hessian)))
grid <- expand.grid(
  mu = seq(mode_fit$par[1] - 7 * local_sd[1],
           mode_fit$par[1] + 7 * local_sd[1], length.out = 321L),
  log_sigma = seq(mode_fit$par[2] - 7 * local_sd[2],
                  mode_fit$par[2] + 7 * local_sd[2], length.out = 321L)
)
grid$log_kernel <- apply(grid, 1, log_target)
grid$weight <- exp(grid$log_kernel - log_sum_exp(grid$log_kernel))
grid$sigma <- exp(grid$log_sigma)
grid_mean <- colSums(grid[, c("mu", "log_sigma")] * grid$weight)
centered <- sweep(as.matrix(grid[, c("mu", "log_sigma")]),
                  2, grid_mean, "-")
grid_covariance <- crossprod(centered * sqrt(grid$weight))
transform <- t(chol(grid_covariance))
inverse_transform <- solve(transform)

log_target_z <- function(z) log_target(grid_mean + drop(transform %*% z))
gradient_z <- function(z) {
  drop(t(transform) %*% gradient_log_target(grid_mean + drop(transform %*% z)))
}
record_state <- function(step, q, momentum) {
  parameter_pair <- grid_mean + drop(transform %*% q)
  potential <- -log_target_z(q)
  kinetic <- sum(momentum^2) / 2
  data.frame(step, mu = parameter_pair[1], sigma = exp(parameter_pair[2]),
             potential, kinetic, hamiltonian = potential + kinetic)
}

set.seed(2026101805)
epsilon <- .20
L <- 12L
q <- drop(inverse_transform %*% (mode_fit$par - grid_mean))
momentum <- rnorm(2)
path <- vector("list", L + 1L)
path[[1]] <- record_state(0L, q, momentum)
momentum <- momentum + .5 * epsilon * gradient_z(q)
for (step in seq_len(L)) {
  q <- q + epsilon * momentum
  if (step < L) momentum <- momentum + epsilon * gradient_z(q)
  else momentum <- momentum + .5 * epsilon * gradient_z(q)
  path[[step + 1L]] <- record_state(step, q, momentum)
}
path <- do.call(rbind, path)
energy_error <- tail(path$hamiltonian, 1) - path$hamiltonian[1]
acceptance_probability <- min(1, exp(-energy_error))

stopifnot(length(y) == 55L, abs(energy_error) < .001)
data.frame(step_size = epsilon, leapfrog_steps = L,
           energy_error, acceptance_probability)
```

```{r}
#| label: plot-provo-hmc-trajectory
#| fig-cap: "A 12-step leapfrog path through the passage-level Student-t posterior. Contours come from the normalized grid; the two accent points are the trajectory endpoints."
grid$relative_density <- exp(grid$log_kernel - max(grid$log_kernel))
ggplot(grid, aes(mu, sigma, z = relative_density)) +
  geom_contour(color = "grey65", bins = 7, linewidth = .45) +
  geom_path(data = path, aes(mu, sigma), color = "#8B1A1A",
            linewidth = .75, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  geom_point(data = path[c(1, nrow(path)), ], aes(mu, sigma),
             color = "#8B1A1A", size = 1.7, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "Passage-level contrast (mu)",
       y = "Passage contrast scale (sigma)") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

The energy error is `r sprintf("%.6f", energy_error)` and the corresponding acceptance probability is `r sprintf("%.6f", acceptance_probability)`. These values assess this numerical trajectory; they are not probabilities that the linguistic model is true.

We choose $\epsilon=.20$ and $L=12$ because this combination produces a twelve-step trajectory with energy error below $.001$ for the present posterior. A smaller $\epsilon$ would usually improve numerical accuracy at greater computational cost, while changing $L$ would change how far the proposal travels. These values are neither estimated corpus properties nor settings that can be transferred to another posterior without checking its geometry.

## Recap and forward link

1. Potential energy is the negative log posterior kernel; momentum is an auxiliary proposal variable.
2. Gradients steer proposals along local target geometry.
3. Leapfrog's two half momentum steps make the numerical map reversible and volume preserving.
4. The accept--reject correction handles finite-step energy error.

The [mass-matrix page](mass-matrix-geometry.qmd#general-kinetic-energy) now develops the whitening transformation used in this demonstration.

## Check your understanding

1. Which energy contains the posterior kernel?
2. Why is momentum temporary?
3. Which two gradient evaluations enter a leapfrog step?
4. What does the final accept--reject step correct?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. The potential energy $U(q)=-\log\widetilde f(q\mid\mathbf y)$ contains the posterior kernel. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. Momentum is an auxiliary variable used to construct a proposal; integrating it out leaves the marginal posterior for $q$ unchanged. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. A leapfrog step evaluates $\nabla U(q_t)$ before the position update and $\nabla U(q_{t+1})$ after it. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. The final HMC accept--reject step corrects the small Hamiltonian error introduced by numerical leapfrog integration, preserving the target distribution. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>
